Architecture Options for Intelligent Apps

The anatomy of intelligent apps: understand the components, compare the patterns, and choose an architecture that fits the task.

Browse all 20 slides

From individual capabilities to complete applications

The presentation uses a human-body analogy: the LLM is the brain, RAG is a library, tools are hands, MCP is the nervous system, Skills are muscle memory, and guardrails are the immune system. A goal-driven loop brings these capabilities together into an agent; coordinated specialists form a multi-agent system.

Its central recommendation is to add complexity only when the use case requires it. The slides cover component definitions, architecture trade-offs, enterprise examples, review questions and a staged adoption roadmap.

Architecture comparison

ArchitectureUse caseDesign focus
Prompted LLMDrafting, summarizing and transforming supplied contentInstructions, examples and output evaluation
RAG assistantAnswers grounded in selected documentsRetrieval quality, citations and access control
Tool-using assistantReading live data and performing permitted actionsAPI integration, permissions and action approval
WorkflowRepeatable processes with known stepsDefined stages, checks and exception handling
AgentTasks whose next steps depend on observationsGoal-driven tool loop, stopping rules and monitoring
Multi-agent systemWork that benefits from specialist responsibilitiesDelegation, coordination and traceability

Why the architecture choice matters

Read slide text
Why the architecture choice matters Over-building is now the most common way AI projects fail Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 2 >40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. ~130 of the thousands of vendors selling 'agentic AI' offer real agentic capability, by Gartner's estimate. The rest is 'agent washing'. 33% of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. The choice is coming either way. Source: Gartner, June 2025 press release and forecasts. The lesson: match the architecture to the problem Anthropic found the most successful teams build with simple, composable patterns rather than complex frameworks. Every step up in autonomy adds capability, and adds cost, latency and risk to govern.

Slide 4 of 20

LLM = the brain

Read slide text
LLM = the brain Reasoning and language, but no memory of you and no hands Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 4 LLM · large language model The brain A brilliant generalist that has read much of the internet. It reasons, writes and summarises, but knows only what it learned in training and forgets each conversation when it ends. WHAT IT IS • A model trained on vast text to understand and generate language • Used through a chat app or an API • Its context window is working memory for one task WHAT IT ADDS • Reasoning, writing, summarising, translating, coding • Reads text, images and documents you give it • No integration needed: fastest time to value LIMITS • Knowledge frozen at a training cut-off • Doesn't know your company's data • Can state wrong facts confidently • Can't act on anything by itself USE IT FOR • Drafting emails, reports, copy • Summarising documents users paste in • Brainstorming and translation EXAMPLE APP Marketing content assistant Drafts campaign copy in the brand voice from a brief; a strong prompt with examples is all it needs. ANALOGY CHECK Holds for reasoning and language. Breaks on learning: a brain keeps learning, an LLM's knowledge is fixed until the vendor retrains it.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 5 of 20

RAG = the brain + a library

Read slide text
RAG = the brain + a library Fixing the analogy: retrieval is an open-book exam, not memory Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 5 Retrieval-augmented generation The library Before answering, the brain looks up the relevant pages in your own library, then answers from them and cites its sources, like an open-book exam. WHAT IT IS • Search your documents for passages that match the question • Add them to the prompt • The LLM answers grounded in that text WHAT IT ADDS • Answers from current, private knowledge • Citations users can check • Update knowledge by editing documents, not the model LIMITS • Only as good as the documents and the search • Weak on questions that need the whole corpus • Reads, but doesn't act • Must respect access rights USE IT FOR • Policy, HR and IT help desks • Searching contracts, manuals, research • Customer FAQs with sources EXAMPLE APP Employee policy assistant Answers 'How much parental leave do I get in Germany?' from the current HR handbook, with a link to the clause. ANALOGY CHECK Better as a library than as memory. Remembering past conversations and user preferences is a separate memory layer: the diary.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 6 of 20

Customising the brain: instructions, library or education?

Read slide text
Customising the brain: instructions, library or education? Three ways to make a general model work for your business Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 6 Prompting = Instructions CHANGES Nothing in the model: you tell it the role, rules and examples BEST FOR Tone, format and framing of the task EFFORT Hours; the cheapest lever TO UPDATE Edit the text, any time RAG = Library CHANGES What the model can read when it answers BEST FOR Facts, policies and fast-changing knowledge with citations EFFORT Days to weeks; needs search infrastructure TO UPDATE Update the documents Fine-tuning = Education CHANGES The model's own weights BEST FOR Consistent style; narrow, high-volume tasks on cheaper models EFFORT Weeks; needs thousands of good examples TO UPDATE Retrain Rule of thumb: a knowledge problem calls for RAG; a behaviour problem calls for a better prompt first, then fine-tuning. Many production systems use all three.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 7 of 20

Tools = the hands

Read slide text
Tools = the hands Letting the brain look things up and get things done Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 7 Tools · function calling The hands The brain can decide to send an email, but it needs hands to do it. Tools let the LLM call an API, run a query or update a record. WHAT IT IS • Functions the model can ask to run: search, query, create, update • Your systems execute them and return results • The model picks the tool and its inputs WHAT IT ADDS • Live data: orders, stock, calendars • Actions: book, file, update, send • Exact calculations instead of guesses LIMITS • Each system needs an integration • A wrong action has real consequences • Needs permissions, logs and approvals USE IT FOR • Copilots that update CRM or tickets • Checking orders, bookings, inventory • Analysis that runs real queries EXAMPLE APP Sales meeting copilot After a call it logs notes in the CRM, moves the deal stage and drafts the follow-up for the rep to approve. ANALOGY CHECK Holds: hands do what the brain decides. Add: these hands can do only what you permit, so grant the least privilege needed.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 8 of 20

MCP = the nervous system

Read slide text
MCP = the nervous system One standard way to wire the brain to every system Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 8 MCP · Model Context Protocol The nerves Nerves carry signals between the brain and every part of the body through one shared system. MCP is that shared wiring between AI apps and your tools and data. Without a standard: 3 × 4 = 12 custom links Chat app Copilot Agent CRM ERP Email Files With MCP: 3 + 4 = 7 standard connections MCP Chat app Copilot Agent CRM ERP Email Files Nov 2024 Launched by Anthropic as an open standard Dec 2025 Donated to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation 10,000+ Active public servers; adopted by ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Cursor and VS Code
Back to slide navigation

Slide 9 of 20

Skills = muscle memory

Read slide text
Skills = muscle memory Packaging how your organisation does things, loaded only when needed Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 9 Agent Skills · SKILL.md Muscle memory A pianist doesn't think about each finger. Skills package proven know-how, such as 'how we write a board report', that the agent loads only when a task calls for it. WHAT IT IS • A folder of instructions, scripts and templates • The agent sees a one-line description until it needs it • Open standard since Dec 2025, used by 30+ agent tools WHAT IT ADDS • Consistent, on-brand, compliant output • Expert procedures captured once, reused everywhere • Keeps the context small: details load on demand LIMITS • Encodes procedure, not judgement • Needs owners, review and versions, like code • Third-party skills can hide risky instructions USE IT FOR • House formats for reports and decks • Finance close, compliance checks • Procedures experts repeat EXAMPLE APP Quarterly business review pack One skill holds the template, metric definitions and checks, so every region's QBR comes out the same way. ANALOGY CHECK Holds: practised routines run without relearning. Add: unlike muscle memory, skills are written down, so they can be reviewed and shared.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 10 of 20

Workflow or agent? Choreography or improvisation

Read slide text
Workflow or agent? Choreography or improvisation The single most important architecture decision Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 10 Workflow = choreography You script the steps; the LLM thinks inside each one Classify Retrieve Draft Check • Predictable, testable, cheaper and faster • Best when the process is known: claims, invoices, onboarding, triage • Common patterns: chaining, routing, parallel steps, reviewer loops Agent = improvisation The LLM chooses the steps and tools as it goes, until the goal is met Plan Act Observe repeat until done • Flexible on open-ended problems • More tokens and latency; harder to test and predict • Best when the path can't be known in advance: research, troubleshooting, coding Default to a workflow. Move to an agent only when the flexibility is worth the extra cost and unpredictability.

Slide 11 of 20

AI agent = brain + hands + memory, in a loop

Read slide text
AI agent = brain + hands + memory, in a loop Fixing the equation: hands aren't enough without a goal and a loop Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 11 Goal Perceive Read the request and context Think Brain plans the next step Act Hands call tools via MCP Remember Store results in memory THE FULL EQUATION Brain LLM reasons and plans Hands tools act in systems Nerves MCP connects them Memory keeps context across steps Muscle memory Skills apply proven procedures Goal + loop keeps going until done or stopped GOOD FITS • Research and analysis • IT and ops troubleshooting • Software development WATCH FOR • Runaway loops and cost • Errors that compound over steps • Actions nobody approved

Slide 12 of 20

Multi-agent system = a team of specialists

Read slide text
Multi-agent system = a team of specialists An orchestrator delegates; A2A is the shared language between agents Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 12 Orchestrator agent Team lead: plans and delegates Research agent Finance agent Compliance agent Supplier's agent (another company) A2A Like a well-run team A lead breaks down the work; specialists own their domains, use their own tools and hand results back. WHEN IT PAYS OFF • Work spans several domains • Different owners or vendors • Too big for one agent's context WHAT IT COSTS • Several times the tokens • More ways to fail • Harder to trace who did what Analogy check: teams add coordination overhead. Use several agents only when one well-equipped agent can't do the job.
Back to slide navigation

Slide 13 of 20

Guardrails = the immune system

Read slide text
Guardrails = the immune system Layered defences that grow with autonomy Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 13 Screen what comes in Detect prompt injection, malicious files and sensitive data in inputs Grant least privilege Tools and data scoped to the user and the task; no standing admin rights Keep a human in the loop Approval for payments, deletions, external messages and other high-impact actions Check what goes out Grounding, policy and format checks before answers reach users or systems Monitor vital signs Evaluations, cost, drift and full audit logs of every step and action The lethal trifecta An agent that has all three can be tricked into leaking data: • Access to private data • Exposure to untrusted content (web, email, files) • A way to send data out Design so at least one leg is missing. Analogy check: an immune system works on its own. AI guardrails must be designed in, tested and owned, and strengthened at every step up in autonomy.

The architecture ladder

Read slide text
The architecture ladder Six levels, from a prompted model to a team of agents Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 14 1 Prompted LLM The brain Draft, summarise, translate 2 RAG assistant + a library Q&A on your documents 3 Tool-using assistant + hands and nerves Look up and update systems via MCP 4 Workflow A choreographed routine Known multi-step processes 5 Agent The whole body in a loop Open-ended tasks, with skills and memory 6 Multi-agent A team Work across domains or companies Climb only as high as the problem needs. Each step adds capability and autonomy, and adds cost, latency and risk to govern. More capability, autonomy, cost and risk

Slide 16 of 20

A decision guide for your next intelligent app

Read slide text
A decision guide for your next intelligent app Start with the brain, then add only what each answer requires Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 16 Start: an LLM with a well-written prompt 1 Must answers come from your own or current knowledge? Yes → Add RAG: the library 2 Must it read live data or take actions in systems? Yes → Add tools via MCP: hands and nerves 3 Can you write down the steps in advance? Yes: build a workflow No: use an agent 4 Do experts repeat the same procedures? Yes → Package them as Skills: muscle memory 5 Does the work span several domains, owners or companies? Yes → Consider multi-agent with A2A: a team Always: guardrails, evaluations, cost limits, and human approval for high-impact actions.

Slide 18 of 20

Eight questions to ask your team

Read slide text
Eight questions to ask your team Use them in every AI architecture review Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 18 Value What decision or task does it improve, and how will we measure it? Simplicity What's the simplest architecture that works? Why not one level lower? Data Which knowledge sources does it use, and who owns their quality and access rights? Actions What can it change in our systems, and which actions need human approval? Security Could it read untrusted content while also reaching private data and sending data out? Evaluation How do we test quality before launch and monitor it afterwards? Cost What does one task cost at scale, and what limits stop runaway loops? Portability Are we building on open standards (MCP, Skills, A2A) to avoid lock-in?

A pragmatic adoption roadmap

Read slide text
A pragmatic adoption roadmap Earn the right to more autonomy with evidence at each stage Anatomy of Intelligent Apps 19 Crawl Typically 0–3 months • LLM and RAG on one high-value knowledge domain • Set up evaluation, logging and an AI risk review • Pick model and platform; adopt MCP for connectors EXIT GATE Measured quality and adoption on real users Walk Typically 3–9 months • Tools via MCP and workflows on one or two processes • Human approval on every action that matters • Start a governed Skills library of house procedures EXIT GATE Processes run reliably with stable cost per task Run Typically 9–18 months • Agents where workflows hit their limits • Multi-agent only where work spans domains • Scale guardrails, monitoring and cost controls EXIT GATE Agents meet quality, safety and ROI targets

Key takeaways

Read slide text
Key takeaways 1 Think in anatomy: LLM brain, RAG library, tools hands, MCP nerves, Skills muscle memory, guardrails immune system. 2 An agent is a loop, not a part: brain, hands and memory pursuing a goal until it's done. 3 Climb the ladder only as far as needed: when the steps are known, a workflow beats an agent. 4 Build on open standards: MCP, Agent Skills and A2A keep components portable across vendors. 5 Scale governance with autonomy: guardrails, evaluations and human approval grow at every step. Frequently asked questions

How should I choose an intelligent-app architecture?

The deck recommends starting with a prompted model and adding capabilities when the task needs them: retrieval for source knowledge, tools for system interaction, and an agent loop when steps cannot be specified in advance.

What is the difference between RAG and memory?

RAG retrieves relevant source material for an answer. Memory retains selected context, preferences or prior work across steps or sessions. The deck compares them to a library and a diary.

How do tools, MCP and Skills differ?

Tools provide operations the application can execute. MCP provides a standard interface for connecting AI applications with tools and data. Skills package instructions, scripts and templates for repeatable procedures.

When does the deck favor a workflow over an agent?

A workflow fits a known sequence of steps. An agent can choose its next steps dynamically. The presentation recommends weighing the need for that flexibility against cost, latency and governance effort.

Is this a rigid ladder that every app must climb?

No. The ladder is a teaching model. Applications can combine retrieval, tools, procedures and workflows without requiring every component or adopting multiple agents.
